## Solution

**Answer: No.** The set $X$ need not have finite index in $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$.

### Counterexample

Let 
$$G = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{\infty} \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z},$$
the direct sum of countably many copies of $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, viewed as an $\mathbb{F}_2$-vector space $V$ with basis $\{e_1, e_2, e_3, \dots\}$. Since $G$ is abelian, every subgroup is normal. The automorphism group of $G$ is
$$\operatorname{Aut}(G) = \operatorname{GL}(V),$$
the group of all invertible $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear maps $V \to V$ (group homomorphisms coincide with $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear maps here).

Define the subgroup
$$K = \operatorname{span}\{e_2, e_3, e_4, \dots\} = \{v \in V : \text{the } e_1\text{-coordinate of } v \text{ is } 0\}.$$
This is a codimension-$1$ subspace, so $[G:K] = 2 < \infty$, and $K \trianglelefteq G$ (as $G$ is abelian).

### The stabilizer and its orbit

The set $X = \{\varphi \in \operatorname{Aut}(G) : \varphi(K) = K\}$ is the stabilizer of $K$ under the natural action of $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ on the set of subgroups of $G$. By the **orbit–stabilizer theorem**,
$$[\operatorname{Aut}(G) : X] = |\operatorname{Orb}(K)|.$$

The orbit of $K$ consists of all $\varphi(K)$ for $\varphi \in \operatorname{GL}(V)$. Since $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ acts transitively on the set of codimension-$1$ subspaces (hyperplanes) of $V$, the orbit of $K$ is exactly the set of **all hyperplanes** of $V$.

### The orbit is infinite

For each $i \geq 1$, the subspace
$$H_i = \{v \in V : \text{the } e_i\text{-coordinate of } v \text{ is } 0\}$$
is a hyperplane, and $H_i \neq H_j$ for $i \neq j$. Hence there are infinitely many hyperplanes (in fact uncountably many, since the algebraic dual $V^*$ has uncountable dimension over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and hyperplanes are in bijection with nonzero linear functionals up to scalar—over $\mathbb{F}_2$ the only scalar is $1$).

Therefore
$$[\operatorname{Aut}(G) : X] = |\operatorname{Orb}(K)| = \infty.$$

### Conclusion

The stabilizer $X$ of $K$ in $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ has **infinite index**, even though $K$ is a normal subgroup of finite index. Thus the statement is **false** in general: $X$ need not have finite index in $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$.

### PROOF COMPLETE

So the question reduces to: is the orbit of K finite? I.e., are there only finitely many normal subgroups of G that are images of K under automorphisms?

Each φ(K) is a normal subgroup of G (since automorphisms preserve normality) of the same index n as K (since automorphisms preserve index... well, φ(K) has index equal to [G:φ(K)] = [G:K] = n since φ is a bijection).

So the orbit of K is contained in the set of normal subgroups of G of index n. Is that set finite?

A group can have infinitely many normal subgroups of a given finite index n. For example, G = Z (infinite cyclic). Normal subgroups of index n: only nZ, so just one. That's finite.

It has finitely many subgroups of index n (finite number of subgroups of given index in finitely generated group—actually the number of subgroups of index n in a finitely generated group is finite). Yes: a finitely generated group has only finitely many subgroups of a given finite index, because each such subgroup corresponds to a transitive permutation representation of degree n, and Hom(G, S_n) is finite when G is finitely generated.

Therefore the answer is: No, X need not have finite index in Aut(G).

Let me make this concrete and rigorous.

Let G = ⊕_{i=1}^∞ Z/2Z, viewed as an F_2-vector space V with basis e_1, e_2, …. This is an abelian group, so every subgroup is normal. Aut(G) = GL(V), the group of invertible linear transformations of V (as F_2-vector space). Actually, for infinite-dimensional vector spaces, GL(V) is the group of all invertible linear maps V → V.

Let K = span{e_2, e_3, …} = {v ∈ V : the e_1-coordinate is 0}. This is a subgroup (subspace) of index 2 (codimension 1), hence normal of finite index.

The set X = {φ ∈ Aut(G) : φ(K) = K} is the stabilizer of the hyperplane K.

The orbit of K under Aut(G) is the set of all codimension-1 subspaces (hyperplanes) of V, since GL(V) acts transitively on hyperplanes.

The algebraic dual V* has dimension 2^{ℵ_0} (uncountable), so there are uncountably many hyperplanes).

Regardless, there are infinitely many hyperplanes. So the orbit is infinite, and [Aut(G) : X] = |orbit| = infinite.

Hence X does not have finite index in Aut(G).

This gives a clean counterexample. Let me write it up.

Actually let me double check: is Aut of the direct sum equal to GL of the vector space? G = (Z/2Z)^{(ℕ)} is an F_2-vector space. Group homomorphisms G → G are F_2-linear maps. Automorphisms of the group = invertible F_2-linear maps = GL(V). Yes.

And the orbit-stabilizer theorem: for a group acting on a set, the index of the stabilizer equals the size of the orbit. This holds even for infinite groups/orbits (as cardinal arithmetic, [G:Stab] = |Orbit|). So [Aut(G):X] = |Orbit(K)| = ∞.
